rationale: A wins because it usually shows its homework before it starts selling the story. Its best discipline is in lines like "whether Mercury Personal is being pitched first to existing business customers/founders or to the open market," which keeps a tempting cross-sell claim as a proof question. B has sharper raw material, but "Two Years After SVB" and "It Just Started Pitching Them Personally" are the kind of confident overclaims that get a founder embarrassed on a reporter call.
gaps_in_A: "The bank Silicon Valley Bank's collapse built is becoming a mass-market consumer bank" overcredits the SVB collapse and overstates an invite-only checking/savings launch into a mass-market consumer bank.

"Mercury will hold consumer deposits without holding a bank charter itself" is sloppy: the update says partner banks provide banking services, so the headline implies the wrong deposit holder before the body cleans it up.
"well-capitalized, previously B2B-only player" adds a financial condition the update did not give. Profitable and 200,000 business customers are not the same as well-capitalized.
"ready to be a full-service bank" overstates the product and the structure. Checking and savings through partner banks is not full-service, and Mercury does not have a bank charter.
gaps_in_B: "Two Years After SVB" is an invented time peg and, on the public timeline, wrong. If the date is off in the headline, the rest of the pitch starts in a ditch.
"Mercury's name recognition was built entirely on being the startup-banking alternative" turns "became well known" into "entirely." That is unnecessary embroidery.

"Mercury Has 200,000 Business Customers. It Just Started Pitching Them Personally." asserts a cross-sell motion the update does not state. The angle is good; the headline writes a check the facts cannot cash.
"opposite to the consumer-to-business neobank trajectory most competitors have tried" imports a market-history claim without support from the update. Either prove it with comparables or cut it.
